title: Adapter: AutomationBench (Harbor PR #2236) - review notes parity ranges 'touch only at a single endpoint' on a noise-dominated metric
summary: Bot review comments (2026-07-15/16) recompute mean +/- SEM from 3 runs per side, confirm partial_credit ranges overlap, and flag that task_completed_correctly ranges [0.0067,0.0267] vs [0.0267,0.04] overlap only at one endpoint with Harbor systematically higher, on 1-6 passes out of 150 ('noise-dominated'); the item was resolved by adding a noise caveat to the README.
why: Touches the weakness of boundary-touching overlap and sparse pass/fail metrics at k=3, but only as a review nit; no statistical treatment.

title: Adapter: GDB (GraphicDesignBench) (harbor PR #1433) — README notes strict range overlap fails when one side is near-deterministic
summary: Adapter author (Mohit Garg) applied the range-overlap criterion to 39 sub-benchmarks: 35 match, 4 do not. README text: '4 NO rows ... have tight non-overlapping ranges — one side (typically upstream) is near-deterministic across its 3 runs and differs from the other side by a small but consistent offset. Mean deltas are all <= 0.12 in reward space, but because neither side's run-to-run variation covers the gap, strict range overlap fails. Running more runs per ...' Approved and merged by Slimshilin without changing the rule.
why: An empirical, in-the-wild observation of the property we formalise (the verdict depends on within-side spread, not on the size of the gap; low-variance ports are penalised, noisy ports rewarded). It is a one-paragraph README remark, not an analysis, but a reviewer could cite it as 'already known'.

title: Add evidence-based adapter review skill (adapters PR #7, OPEN) — parity-diagnostics reference
summary: Open PR by audreina17 adding skills/review-adapter/SKILL.md and references/parity-diagnostics.md. The diff instructs reviewers to 'Recompute the reported statistics from original_runs and harbor_runs ... mean and sample SEM, and overlapping run-score ranges. SEM is undefined for one run. Do not substitute overlapping SEM intervals or close means for the repository's range-overlap criterion. Meeting that criterion does not waive fidelity checks or establish general equivalence.' One comment (anson627: lgtm).
why: A maintainer-side document explicitly concedes that passing the range-overlap criterion does not 'establish general equivalence', which is close to our thesis in words, but it proposes no alternative test and performs no analysis. Worth citing as evidence the gap is recognised internally.

title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard
summary: Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards applied to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor-Index task-level outcome data. Finds model-scaffold systems rank reliably but underlying models do not; scaffold choice can change conclusions; more tasks cannot fix scaffold-limited uncertainty.
why: The only paper found that statistically re-analyses published Harbor data. Read in full: it uses Harbor-Index task-level scores for a pooled corroboration analysis and never mentions parity experiments, adapters/ports, range overlap, or equivalence testing. Nearest neighbour; cite and differentiate, but it does not do what we plan.

title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard
summary: Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse agent leaderboards applied to 30,859 rollouts from 9 HAL benchmarks plus 13 Harbor Index benchmarks; separates model, benchmark and scaffold effects, finds fixed model-scaffold systems rank reliably (0.935-0.994) while underlying-model reliability is much lower (0.148-0.841), and that more tasks cannot fix scaffold-dominated uncertainty. Full text mentions Harbor 12 times (as a data source); the only 'parity' occurrence is 'structural parity' in a figure caption; no analysis of parity experiments or ports.
why: Uses Harbor Index data and quantifies scaffold-induced noise, so reviewers may cite it as 'already analysing Harbor data'; it does not touch the adapter parity experiments or the matching criterion.

title: AgentCompass: A Unified Evaluation Infrastructure for Agent Capabilities
summary: Open-source infrastructure separating Benchmark, Harness and Environment, natively supporting 20+ benchmarks across five capability dimensions, with fault-tolerant async runtime and trajectory analysis.
why: Re-implements 20+ benchmarks (ports) without any stated fidelity/parity check in the abstract; relevant as another port collection whose validation practice could be contrasted with Harbor's.

title: Align adapter CI and documentation around a versioned contract (adapters PR #3, OPEN)
summary: Open PR by anson627 that makes docs/adapters.mdx a versioned contract and adds machine checks: 'ADP-PARITY | At least two runs per side and matching run ranges', 'ADP-STATS | Mean and sample SEM calculated from raw run arrays'; validator emits 'ADP-PARITY: insufficient runs' when a side has <2 runs, and a unit test recomputes mean and stdev/sqrt(n). PR body: 'Compared affected checks across all 85 existing adapters: errors unchanged. Added warnings: 46 insufficient-run findings and one unsupported cost type.' No equivalence test, CI, or margin.
why: Touches run-count adequacy and encodes the range-overlap rule in CI, but only as a structural check (n>=2). The '46 of 85 adapters flagged insufficient-run' number is a useful fact for contribution (2). No statistical re-analysis.

title: Benchmark Scores Are Pipeline-Dependent: A Reliability Audit of Cybersecurity LLM Benchmarks
summary: Audits 8 cybersecurity benchmarks x 10 LLMs treating each benchmark as a measurement pipeline; identifies 15 failure modes; a single pipeline choice can shift a model's score by >80 points and reorder models; under a standardized harness 9/10 models shift >=3 ranks on at least one benchmark. No agreement/equivalence statistics seen in abstract.
why: Systematic measurement of harness/pipeline-vs-original gaps (the port-versus-original question), in a different domain and without equivalence testing or parity data.

title: Beyond Metrics: A Critical Analysis of the Variability in Large Language Model Evaluation Frameworks
summary: Critical analysis of LLM evaluation frameworks; search snippet reports it compares OpenCompass and EleutherAI's harness and finds the same model scores very differently on the same dataset depending on scoring method (up to ~26%).
why: Prior cross-framework discrepancy study (same benchmark, different implementation); no statistical equivalence framework. The abstract page is vague; details come from a search snippet.

title: CUBE: A Standard for Unifying Agent Benchmarks
summary: Position/standard proposal: a protocol on MCP and Gym so benchmarks are 'wrapped once and used everywhere', separating task/benchmark/package/registry layers to remove the per-benchmark 'integration tax'.
why: Touches benchmark ports directly but proposes no validation that a wrapped benchmark matches the original; a citation, not a competitor.

title: Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit
summary: Audits 17 'compressed model is equivalent to original' claims (none states a prospective numerical equivalence margin, none releases task-matched per-item outputs); shows per-item churn is ~5x the net accuracy delta across 1,707 model-by-task cells; proposes paired equivalence testing at a declared margin with sample-size tables and a 5-part reporting standard (declare margin, run paired test, report churn beside net delta, state n, release per-item outputs).
why: Closest methodological precedent to our contributions (2)-(3): same argument (a small aggregate delta is weak evidence of sameness; demand a declared margin, paired per-item equivalence test, sample-size table) but applied to model compression, not benchmark ports or Harbor parity. We should cite it and position ports as a new application; it does not touch the range-overlap rule.

title: Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit (arXiv 2608.15046)
summary: Argues small net accuracy deltas are weak evidence of equivalence; measures per-item 'churn' (~5x net delta) across 1,707 model-task cells; audits 16 equivalence claims (method papers, model cards, vendor docs) and finds none states a prospective numerical margin or releases per-item outputs; proposes paired TOST at a declared margin (primary ±2 pp; also ±1, ±3), paired sd=sqrt(p_d), required-n tables (e.g. MMLU 2,164 items at ±2 pp), and a 5-part reporting standard (declare margin, paired test, churn beside delta, n, per-item outputs). Appendix H documents lm-eval harness sensitivity (GSM8K filter 0.232 vs 0.566). Does not mention Harbor, Inspect, ports, or range overlap.
why: Closest methodological precedent: 'equivalence test with stated margin + paired per-item analysis + runs/items needed + audit of equivalence claims' is the same recipe as contributions (2)-(3), applied to compressed-vs-original models instead of harness ports. The paper's novelty must rest on the port/parity setting and the critique of range overlap, not on introducing TOST or paired analysis to LLM evals.

title: Certifying Model Upgrades with Slice-Wise Non-Regression and Incumbent Fallback
summary: Distinguishes 'failing to detect harm' from 'certifying non-inferiority' for model upgrades; in simulation a no-detected-harm gate released a harmful candidate in 99.7% of trials vs 2.6% for an exact non-inferiority gate; proposes paired evaluation with finite-sample guarantees and fallback to the incumbent when certification fails.
why: Makes the same logical argument we make about range overlap (a test that only fails to detect a difference is not evidence of sameness) using non-inferiority tests, in the model-release setting rather than benchmark ports.

title: Claude 4.5+ & gpt5.4 models doing too well on Swebenchpro (Harbor issue #1067)
summary: Users found the SWE-bench Pro adapter baked gold test files into the Docker image; agents read them in 56-90% of tasks and scored ~30 pp above official baselines (Opus-4.5 71.7% vs official 45.89 ± 3.60). Maintainer robertzhidealx: 'Very strange that our prior parity experiments didn't catch it'. Fix merged same day; a re-run parity experiment was requested.
why: A documented case where a passed parity experiment missed a large systematic adaptation error — strong motivating evidence for the paper, not prior work that overlaps it.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
summary: Corrected citation: Fengshuo Liu, Ying Liu, Ruize Sun, Lie Luo, Siyuan Guo. arXiv:2609.17394, v1 15 Sep 2026; accepted at ADMA 2026 (Special Session on Responsible Data Intelligence), 15 pp. Audits 254 SWE-bench submissions without running models: top entries share most successes (nesting 0.935), within-model scaffold ranges reach 29.8 pp, exact paired McNemar tests separate none of 29 adjacent Verified top-30 pairs. Releases a five-step 'resolution audit' protocol on per-instance verdict matrices and an instance-budget formula. Explicitly states 'non-rejection does not establish equivalence or non-inferiority: we specify no practical equivalence margin' and that its tiers are not evidence of equivalence. (a) Harbor parity: NO. (b) Ports/re-implementations: NO (compares leaderboard entries on one harness). (c) Equivalence testing: touched conceptually (names the equivalence/non-inferiority gap as a limitation) but does not perform TOST.
why: Does not re-analyse parity data or critique Harbor, but it is the nearest prior work on paired per-task significance testing of agent results and it names the missing equivalence margin; our paired per-task TOST analysis should be positioned as filling exactly the gap it declines to fill.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
summary: Audits 254 SWE-bench submissions without running models: exact paired McNemar tests separate none of 29 adjacent top-30 Verified pairs; within-model scaffold ranges reach 29.8 points; proposes a five-step audit protocol including estimating the instance budget needed for resolution. Full text states 'Non-rejection does not establish equivalence or non-inferiority: we specify no practical equivalence margin.'
why: Methodologically adjacent to contribution (3) (paired per-task tests, sample-size for resolution, explicit awareness of the equivalence gap) but applied to leaderboard ordering, not to benchmark ports or parity.

title: Developing and Maintaining an Open-Source Repository of AI Evaluations: Challenges and Insights (Inspect Evals)
summary: Eight months of maintaining inspect_evals (70+ ported evaluations); proposes cohort-based contribution management, statistical methods for resampling and cross-model comparison with uncertainty quantification, and QA processes for reproducibility. Abstract does not describe validating ports against original baselines statistically.
why: The other large port collection; relevant for related work on how ports are validated in practice (Inspect's CONTRIBUTING.md only requires that baseline results exist 'so we can validate that your implementation produces similar performance', with no stated criterion).

title: Developing and Maintaining an Open-Source Repository of AI Evaluations: Challenges and Insights (inspect_evals)
summary: Eight months of maintaining inspect_evals (70+ community evaluations). Proposes cohort management for contributions, 'statistical methodologies for optimal resampling and cross-model comparison with uncertainty quantification', and quality-control processes for reproducibility; search snippet mentions stratified sampling to cut validation cost.
why: The Inspect Evals analogue of Harbor's parity validation; if its full text compares re-implementations to original reported scores with a stated criterion, it narrows contribution 3. Abstract does not state such a criterion; the full text is covered in the next row and in phase1_verdicts.csv.

title: Developing and Maintaining an Open-Source Repository of AI Evaluations: Challenges and Insights (inspect_evals; arXiv 2507.06893)
source: arXiv (cs.CL); Abbas, Waggoner, Olive (Arcadia Impact / inspect_evals maintainers)
summary: Sec 3.3.1: 'Frontier models are run on evaluation subsets to verify that results match reference implementations within +/-5% deviation'; 'Deviations require investigation' (usually missing temperature/endpoint details). Sec 3.4: subsets of max $100 or 10-20% of data. Sec 3.5-3.6: resampling via epochs (Miller's rule) and paired cross-model comparison with 95% CIs.
why: A published, fixed tolerance (±5%) for accepting a benchmark re-implementation in a major harness; directly narrows any 'first stated margin for ports' framing and belongs in the related-work table. No equivalence test, no port-vs-original statistics beyond the threshold.

title: Equivalence hypothesis testing in experimental software engineering (Dolado, Otero, Harman)
summary: Title and bibliographic record only: proposes equivalence hypothesis testing for software-engineering experiments (8 citations per OpenAlex). Abstract could not be retrieved (the Springer page was not accessible; the EHU repository record has no abstract).
why: Direct precedent for equivalence testing in empirical SE experiments and replications; does not concern ML benchmarks or ports. The abstract and reference list were later checked; see extra_verifications/se_equivalence_refs.md.

title: Every Eval Ever: A Unifying Schema and Community Repository for AI Evaluation Results (arXiv 2606.14516)
summary: Batzner et al. Section 7.3 reproduces three models on fourteen single-turn HELM benchmarks and compares aligned per-instance scores between official HELM records and local reproductions; match = identical score 'up to numerical tolerance' (value unstated). Reported agreement mostly >93%, WikiFact ~92%, lowest ~79% for Falcon-7B on one benchmark. Motivation: frameworks 'produce divergent scores for nominally identical evaluations'. No statistical test.
why: A systematic original-vs-rerun comparison with a stated (instance-level, exact) matching rule; related work for contribution (2) but orthogonal to score-level equivalence testing and to Harbor.

title: Every Eval Ever: A Unifying Schema and Community Repository for AI Evaluation Results (arXiv 2606.14516) — reproduces 14 HELM benchmarks and compares per-instance to official records
summary: Abstract notes frameworks 'produce divergent scores for nominally identical evaluations'. Per search snippets of the full text, a case study reran 3 models on 14 HELM benchmarks and reported share of aligned per-instance scores that match (e.g., ~92% on WikiFact), tracing mismatches to row-order changes and serving artifacts; descriptive agreement rates, no equivalence test. Abstract page read; full text only via snippets.
why: Closest systematic 'reimplementation vs original' comparison found; different object (HELM re-runs, not agentic ports) and no TOST. Could narrow the novelty of contribution (2) if the paper claimed to be first to compare re-implementations statistically; it does not.

title: General Agent Evaluation
summary: Unifying protocol and harness that surfaces any benchmark to any general-purpose agent (explicitly contrasts with Harbor's CLI-only protocol); full factorial of 5 architectures x 5 LLMs x 6 benchmarks; claims top general agents are 'indistinguishable' from domain-specific agents on 4/6 benchmarks.
why: Another benchmark-porting/unification effort that names Harbor; abstract gives no port-validation or equivalence procedure, but full text may contain its own parity-like check.

title: General Agent Evaluation (Exgentic harness; ports 6 benchmarks and 5 agents into one harness)
date: 2026-02-26 (v1); 2026-05-11 (v2); ICLR 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild
summary: Bandel et al. (IBM). Builds a Unified Protocol and harness that 'surfaces any benchmark to any general-purpose agent and backbone model', wrapping original benchmark code as black boxes; full factorial of 5 architectures x 5 LLMs x 6 benchmarks. Abstract reports architecture choice shifts results up to 12 points. The abstract does not mention any check that the wrapped benchmarks reproduce original scores; full text not read.
why: A multi-benchmark porting effort by a different group. If the full paper contains a score-reproduction check it is prior art for 'validating ports'; if it does not, it is an example of ports shipped without parity evidence, which supports our motivation. The full text was read later; see the phase1_verdicts.csv row for arXiv 2602.22953.

title: Generality Labs inspect-evals-template CONTRIBUTING.md: Evaluation Report and 'Comparing your results' protocol
summary: Linked from inspect_evals CONTRIBUTING. 'Your implementation needs to be compared against the original paper or an existing reputable leaderboard result'; recommends >=2 models, full dataset or a 20-30% representative subset if cost >~$100; report must list deviations from reference implementations, comparison table, timestamp, exact commands. No numeric tolerance or statistical test.
why: Current written port-validation protocol for Inspect Evals: qualitative, no margin; useful contrast row for the related-work table.

title: Harbor ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md debug playbook: per-task 'overlap analysis' and noise-vs-systematic classification
summary: Beyond the Step-5 range-overlap criterion (max(A)>=min(B) and max(B)>=min(A); 'Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match'), the 'Debug playbook' table (step 3: 'Per-task resolution on each side; list tasks resolved on A-only and on B-only'; step 4: tasks that flip vs. fail every run; step 5: rerun high-variance tasks 5-10 times) prescribes informal per-task diagnostics when ranges do not overlap. Definition section states scores 'should be statistically indistinguishable'.
why: Per-task diagnosis is already recommended by the maintainers, though only as a fallback when the range test fails and without any statistic; the paper should cite this rather than claim per-task analysis is absent from Harbor's protocol.

title: Harbor ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md: 'Definition' ('statistically indistinguishable'), 'Matching criterion' (range overlap iff) and 'Debug playbook' step 3 'Overlap analysis' (per-task A-only/B-only split)
summary: Verified current text: 'scores on both sides should be statistically indistinguishable'; 'The two sides match if and only if their run-score ranges overlap: max(A) >= min(B) AND max(B) >= min(A)'; 'Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match'; SEM 'shrinks as runs are added'. Debug playbook step 3: 'Per-task resolution on each side; list tasks resolved on A-only and on B-only. A roughly symmetric split suggests sampling noise... A lopsided split suggests systematic adaptation error'; step 4 distinguishes tasks that flip across runs from tasks that fail on one side every run; step 5 says run high-variance tasks 5-10 times in isolation. The same text is duplicated in harbor-framework/adapters docs/adapters.mdx (AI guide). The newer human guide docs/adapters-human.mdx (repo created 2026-09-09) drops the overlap sentence entirely and says only results 'should be comparable to demonstrate equivalence', reported as mean +/- sample SEM.
why: Two things for the paper: (1) the maintainers' debug playbook already contains an informal paired per-task analysis (A-only vs B-only counts, symmetric vs lopsided), so contribution 3 should be framed as formalising it (McNemar/paired bootstrap with a margin) rather than introducing the idea; (2) the human-facing guide now states no criterion at all while the AI guide and harbor repo keep 'iff overlap' — the paper's sentence 'the check Harbor uses' must cite the exact file and date.

title: Harbor Adapters & Harbor Index @CAIS AgenticSE Workshop (Lin Shi talk, YouTube, 28 min)
summary: The Harbor adapters team lead presents the adapter program and the parity protocol (10:00-15:30). He says the team does not trust reported scores and reruns both sides itself; describes three scenarios (original has a Harbor-supported agent; original is vanilla-LLM so contributors must fork it and add an agent; original has a custom agent that must be added to Harbor); and states the acceptance philosophy as identical agent+model, "three to five runs to average out the variance", and an overlap check on mean plus/minus a deviation (ASR renders it as 'mean personal deviation'). He says debugging a parity mismatch can take tens to hundreds of hours and claims the process is more rigorous than any existing community work. No critique of the criterion, no statistics beyond that, no re-analysis.
why: Directly about the parity criterion and from the person who runs it, so it must be cited; but it only states (a third, inconsistent formulation of) the rule, it does not question its power or re-analyse the data. Useful as evidence that the stated rule varies between guide (range overlap), paper (SEM) and talk (mean +/- deviation overlap, 3-5 runs).

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index (arXiv 2609.04298 v3) - two adapters already use significance tests for parity
summary: Full-text search: Appendix D.4 defines k=3 runs, mean +/- SEM, and 'passes parity when the original and Harbor means agree within a margin consistent with their standard errors'; the per-benchmark notes say SciCode parity has 'sub-step accuracy aligned within a Welch t-test' and the 479-task data-science coding adapter (DA-Agent, 3 trials) reports 'a permutation test shows no statistically significant difference'. The paper cites none of Tukey, Neave & Granger, Schenker & Gentleman, Payton, Cumming & Finch or Belia, and never mentions Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, TOST or equivalence testing beyond the phrase 'statistical equivalence ... within sample SEM'.
why: This detail matters for the novelty framing: the maintainers already treat a non-significant Welch/permutation test as parity evidence in two adapters, i.e. the absence-of-evidence fallacy the TOST contribution corrects. No statistical critique of the overlap rule inside the paper.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index paper, arXiv 2609.04298 v3 (Appendix D.4.2 criterion wording; D.7 'statistical equivalence ... within sample SEM'; one SciCode entry mentions a Welch t-test)
summary: The full text confirms: k=3 default, mean ± SEM, 'passes parity when the original and Harbor means agree within a margin consistent with their standard errors'; D.7: 'must confirm statistical equivalence with the original benchmark within sample SEM'. One benchmark entry (SciCode) says 'sub-step accuracy aligned within a Welch t-test'. No equivalence test, CI, or power statement; criterion wording differs from the repo's range-overlap rule.
why: The target work; contains no self-critique and no re-analysis. The Welch t-test mention shows the authors treat non-rejection as parity in at least one case.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation
summary: Confirmed from the abs page submission history: v1 Thu 3 Sep 2026 16:26 UTC; v2 Wed 9 Sep 2026 15:25 UTC; v3 Thu 10 Sep 2026 02:39 UTC (all 1,195 KB); submitted by Haowei Lin. 126 authors; first authors in order: Lin Shi, Haowei Lin, Zixuan Zhu, Xiaoyue Zhou, Xiang Li, Xiangning Lin, Yaxuan Deng, Han Xu, Yuangang Li, Shanda Li, Zizhao Chen, Hanwen Xing, Harsh Raj, Bo Chen, Quan Shi, Steven Dillmann, Yipeng Gao, Puneesh Khanna, Ruofan Lu, ...; last three: Mike Merrill, Ludwig Schmidt, Alex Shaw. Abstract: adapters port 80+ benchmarks, validated by code review and parity experiments; 8 models x 54 benchmarks; Harbor-Index (82 tasks, 29 benchmarks). Appendix D.4.2 (v3 text): each side run k=3 times by default, mean +/- sample SEM = s/sqrt(k); 'An adapter passes parity when the original and Harbor means agree within a margin consistent with their standard errors.' The adapter-requirements list says verbatim: 'A parity experiment must confirm statistical equivalence with the original benchmark within sample SEM, on a parity set whose composition is recorded in parity_experiment.json.' The phrase 'range overlap' / 'ranges overlap' does not occur anywhere in the paper (the wording comes from adapters/ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md; see the rows for that file). D.4.1 itself concedes ports shift scores by several points and that users 'cannot tell whether a score difference reflects a genuine capability gap, a harness artifact, or a latent bug'. No CI, TOST, power or false-alarm analysis of the criterion appears. (a) Harbor parity: YES (defines it). (b) Ports: YES. (c) Equivalence testing: claims 'statistical equivalence within SEM' as a requirement but applies no formal equivalence test.
why: It is the object of study rather than a competitor: it publishes the parity data and states an SEM-based criterion but does not analyse the criterion's error rates, compute CIs or run TOST. Note the paper's two slightly different wordings and the absence of the range-overlap wording when quoting it.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Mix: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation (NeurIPS 2026 accepted version of arXiv 2609.04298)
date: NeurIPS 2026 (accepted; poster page seen 2026-10-11). OpenReview forum id x9XghoOfwL (inaccessible). Latest arXiv is v3, 2026-09-10.
summary: The maintainers' paper is accepted at NeurIPS 2026 with a changed title: Harbor-Index (82 tasks) became Harbor-Mix (100 tasks; strongest model 15.6%). The accepted abstract still says the 80+ adapters are 'validated through rigorous code review and parity experiments'. No statistical critique in the abstract. The camera-ready PDF and its public reviews (openreview.net/forum?id=x9XghoOfwL) could not be retrieved, and the Wayback Machine has no capture of the forum.
why: This is the target artifact, not a competitor, but (a) the accepted version may have revised Appendix D's parity criterion and run count, and (b) its OpenReview reviews are the single most likely place for a public 'within-SEM at k=3 is not an equivalence test' comment. Neither could be checked. The paper must cite this version; the OpenReview forum (x9XghoOfwL) could not be read.

title: Harbor FeatureBench adapter README / HF parity-experiments commit f5d9fb2: 'Task-level reward agreement: 53/60 (88%)'
date: 2026-03-04 (HF dataset commit; runs 2026-03-02 to 03-04); README last commit 2026-04-24
summary: 30 lite tasks, 2 trials/side, codex gpt-5-mini: original 13.3%±0.0 vs Harbor 15.0%±1.7. Reports per-trial-task reward agreement 53/60 (88%), attributes 7 disagreements to 'stochastic LLM variation, not systematic'. No formal threshold. HF commit URL also seen: https://huggingface.co/datasets/harborframework/parity-experiments/commit/f5d9fb20a25ee29c422e8916e974c8ebc6f2c18b
why: Second adapter record reporting per-task agreement; shows per-task data are already used ad hoc by contributors. A GitHub code search for 'reward agreement' in adapters/ returns only featurebench.

title: Harbor PR #1496 '[Fix] Change std to sample SEM in review bots and tutorials' (merged, introduces range-overlap rule and states 'Within sample SEM alone is neither necessary nor sufficient')
summary: Merged in 15 minutes by crystalxyz. Diff adds to the review-bot checklist and docs: 'The run-score ranges [min, max] on the two sides must overlap per the matching criterion. "Within sample SEM" alone is neither necessary nor sufficient — the required check is range overlap on original_runs vs harbor_runs.' The bot review praises SEM as 'statistically well-motivated'. No statistical justification of range overlap given.
why: Establishes the timeline: the repo adopted range-overlap and explicitly rejected a SEM-margin criterion on 2026-04-22, while the maintainers' paper (2026-09-03) still describes the criterion as 'agree within a margin consistent with their standard errors' / 'statistical equivalence ... within sample SEM' (D.4.2, D.7). This inconsistency is usable in the paper; nobody has pointed it out publicly.

title: Harbor PR #1654 '[Ready for Review] Adapter: asta-bench' - range-overlap cell-count dispute (15/22 vs 17/22) and ranges overlapping only at 0.0
summary: Across five automated review passes on a 2,422-task, 22-cell parity table, the reviewer first counts 15/22 cells passing the range-overlap check, then corrects itself to the author's 17/22, explaining that two cells pass because both sides share a minimum of 0.0 so the ranges trivially overlap at zero. The five non-passing cells are accepted with written structural explanations; the remaining blocker was a missing standard-CLI-agent parity run.
why: Documents two weaknesses of the rule in practice: degenerate overlap at a shared zero, and a pass/fail count that flips between reviews. Again an application, not a critique or statistical re-analysis; supports but does not kill our contribution 1.

title: Harbor PR #1849 'Adapter: CanItEdit' — parity declared on a boundary-touch overlap (121/210)
summary: Original 58.41 ± 0.57 vs Harbor 56.98 ± 0.63 (3 runs each); author: 'ranges overlap at 121/210 (boundary touch — marginal but valid)'. Illustrates that a single shared endpoint passes the rule.
why: Concrete example for the paper that the acceptance rule passes on the thinnest possible overlap; not a critique.

title: Harbor PR #2236 '[Ready for Review] Adapter: AutomationBench' - automated review notes parity ranges touching at a single endpoint
summary: The repo's automated adapter reviewer (claude[bot]) flags that for the strict task_completed_correctly metric the original-side range [0.0067, 0.0267] and Harbor-side range [0.0267, 0.04] overlap only at one endpoint, with Harbor systematically higher (3.11% vs 1.78%), describes the counts (1-6 passes of 150) as noise-dominated, and still marks it acceptable because the primary partial-credit metric matches. Later human review comments (rebekah-west, anson627) do not revisit the criterion.
why: Concrete in-the-wild example that the range-overlap rule admits borderline passes and that reviewers recognise the noise but accept it; it applies the rule rather than critiquing it, and it is bot-generated, so it does not pre-empt our paper. Good anecdote for the motivation section.

title: Harbor PR #2292 'feat: add GitGoodBench adapter' — review-bot comments that the range-overlap criterion is 'trivially/vacuously satisfied' when one run is duplicated into both sides
summary: The repo's Claude review bot wrote: 'Because both sides are literally the same number, the range-overlap matching criterion is trivially satisfied and demonstrates nothing about equivalence between two independent harnesses.' The objection is to a degenerate case (same run on both sides), not to the criterion's power in general; it asks maintainer Lin Shi to confirm the convention. PR still open.
why: Closest thing found to an in-ecosystem critique of the overlap rule, but it is a bot comment about a vacuous special case, not a statistical analysis. Should be cited as evidence the rule is applied mechanically.

title: Harbor PR #408 'PaperBench Adapter: parity-validated integration' — states the overlap test as max(A) >= min(B) AND max(B) >= min(A) and also reports per-paper confidence intervals
summary: Contributor jzheng17 writes the 'range-overlap CI test' formally and additionally reports CIs: '7/8 papers have overlapping CIs at trimmed n=5; mean delta = +0.029', with one paper (bbox) showing disjoint CIs; zero-score failures were excluded before computing n=5-9 per side. Also notes some structured JSON in parity records 'was not trustworthy'.
why: Only contributor-level attempt found to go beyond range overlap (CIs per paper), but it is ad hoc, trims failures, and performs no equivalence test. A data point that practitioners already feel the rule is insufficient.

title: Harbor PR #517: 'harbor stats' CLI — hierarchical bootstrap CI and paired permutation test over result.json files
summary: Adds `harbor stats ci` (hierarchical bootstrap: resample tasks, then trials within task) and `harbor stats diff` (paired permutation test on tasks common to two groups, 10,000 permutations, reports p-value and 'Significant (alpha=0.05)'). Not merged into main (code search for 'Permutation Test'/'Hierarchical Bootstrap' outside adapters/ returns 0 hits), but its output appears verbatim in two adapter parity records (dacode, kramabench).
why: Statistical tooling for Harbor parity comparisons already exists inside the Harbor repo and is used in parity records. It is a difference-detection test ('No statistically significant difference detected'), not an equivalence test, and it does not critique the range-overlap rule, but the paper's framing that nobody can currently tell and that per-task paired analysis is new must acknowledge it.

title: Harbor abc-bench adapter README: per-task overlap, Cohen kappa within-side vs cross-side
summary: Full-benchmark parity (224 tasks, 3 runs/side, codex gpt-5-mini): 45.39±2.48 vs 45.69±0.98. Reports per-task overlap across all 6 rounds (42 always solved, 69 never, 113 stochastic), 'Pairwise exact agreement 72.8-79.5% with Cohen kappa 0.45-0.59; within-side kappa (0.46-0.50) is no higher than cross-side kappa, indicating the platforms agree as well as each agrees with itself'.
why: One adapter already performs the paired per-task analysis with a within-side-vs-cross-side agreement comparison that contribution (3) proposes; no equivalence test and no margin, and it is a single record, but it is a direct precedent in the data the paper re-analyses.

title: Harbor adapters dacode and kramabench parity READMEs: permutation test p-values and bootstrap CIs
summary: Both records run `harbor stats diff` (paired permutation test on common tasks: dacode 479 tasks, p=0.8464; kramabench 104 tasks, p=0.4802) and `harbor stats ci` (hierarchical bootstrap 95% CI, e.g. dacode Harbor 0.389 [0.351, 0.428], width 0.076) and conclude 'No statistically significant difference detected'. labbench and refav READMEs also justify parity by 'overlapping confidence intervals'. A GitHub code search finds 'confidence interval' only in these 4 adapters and 'kappa' only in abc-bench; there are no TOST or equivalence-test hits in adapters/.
why: Shows a minority of parity records already go beyond range overlap with CIs and NHST, using exactly the absence-of-evidence logic the paper would critique; this strengthens contribution (2) but narrows 'no one has applied statistics to parity data'.

title: Harbor adapters spec, Step 5 'Run Parity Experiments' (Matching criterion + Debug playbook) — harbor-framework/adapters docs/adapters.mdx
date: 2026-09-09 (repo split from harbor monorepo; wording dates from 2026-04-19, harbor PR #1403)
summary: Current authoritative contributor spec. Defines parity as 'scores on both sides should be statistically indistinguishable', then sets the matching criterion as pure run-range overlap: max(A)>=min(B) AND max(B)>=min(A); 'Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match'. Requires mean ± sample SEM reporting (>=2 runs, 3+ preferred) and explicitly argues SEM should be used because it 'shrinks as runs are added'. The debug playbook (used only when ranges do not overlap) contains an informal per-task 'Overlap analysis' step: list tasks resolved on A-only vs B-only; 'a roughly symmetric split suggests sampling noise, a lopsided split suggests systematic adaptation error', plus 'run high-variance tasks 5-10 times in isolation'. No hypothesis test, CI, margin, or power/run-count guidance anywhere.
why: This is the object of our critique and also the closest thing to a per-task paired analysis in the maintainers' own material (informal, only triggered on non-overlap). It does not re-analyse data or test the criterion, so it does not kill the paper, but the paper must cite and engage with it (and note the 'statistically indistinguishable' vs 'range overlap' tension inside the same page).

title: Harbor adapters/ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md, Step 5 'Matching criterion' (range overlap iff rule) and 'Reporting format: mean ± sample SEM'
summary: The official rule: 'The two sides match if and only if their run-score ranges overlap ... Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match. Non-overlap should be treated as a systematic adaptation error until evidence indicates otherwise.' Requires >=2 runs per side (3+ preferred), SEM reporting, and a debug playbook including a per-task 'overlap analysis' (A-only vs B-only resolved tasks). No power analysis, CI, or equivalence test.
why: This is the target of contribution (1); it confirms the exact wording and that the maintainers themselves prescribe a per-task overlap analysis only as a debugging step, not as the acceptance test. No critique of the rule exists in the file.

title: Harbor adapters/dacode/parity/README.md and adapters/kramabench/parity/README.md - paired per-task permutation test and hierarchical bootstrap CIs on parity runs
date: 2026-03-30 (dacode, PR #597) and 2026-04-06 (kramabench, PR #469), author Michael Glass
summary: Two adapter parity READMEs run a 'harbor stats diff' permutation test over the common tasks of 3 original vs 3 Harbor runs (dacode: 479 tasks, diff 0.0020, p=0.846; kramabench: 104 tasks, diff 0.0176, p=0.480) and a 'harbor stats ci' hierarchical bootstrap 95% CI per side (10,000 iterations). The 'harbor stats' command is not registered in the current Harbor CLI (src/harbor/cli/main.py has no stats subcommand; no stats module found in history), so it appears to be contributor-local tooling. No equivalence test is used.
why: Shows that paired per-task analysis and bootstrap CIs have already been applied to Harbor parity data for two adapters; it is a significance test (absence of evidence), not TOST, and not systematic across adapters, so it narrows but does not pre-empt contributions (2) and (3). Second URL: https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/adapters/kramabench/parity/README.md

title: Harbor adapters/gdb/README.md parity notes - strict range overlap fails when one side is near-deterministic
summary: GraphicDesignBench adapter parity table: 35/39 sub-benchmarks match by run-score range overlap, 4 do not because 'one side (typically upstream) is near-deterministic across its 3 runs and differs from the other side by a small but consistent offset. Mean deltas are all <= 0.12 ... because neither side's run-to-run variation covers the gap, strict range overlap fails. Running more runs per side would tighten the SEM on each side without changing this structural shape.'
why: A contributor explicitly documents that the overlap rule penalises low-variance sides and that more runs do not help, which is part of our contribution (1) ('rewards noisy ports', 'gets weaker as runs are added'); it is a one-paragraph note, not an analysis, and the contributor reads it as a reason to pass the adapter anyway.

title: Harbor issue #1067 'Claude 4.5+ & gpt5.4 models doing too well on Swebenchpro' (adapter baked gold test files into the image)
summary: Harbor SWE-bench Pro port gave Opus 4.5 71.7% vs official 45.89 ± 3.60 because before_repo_set_cmd checked out gold test files into the container at build time. A port-fidelity failure discovered by users, not by the parity process.
why: Strong motivating example that the port and original can diverge materially; relevant to the claim that the parity check is what should catch this. Not a statistical critique.

title: Harbor upstream: agree live-site oracle evidence and parity acceptance protocol (TIGER-AI-Lab/ClawBench issue #359)
summary: Benchmark authors drafting a Harbor adapter propose a 'parity acceptance protocol': same agents/models/settings, pre-registered task subset, revisions, timeouts, run count, and 'mean ± sample SEM across independent runs' with denominators reported separately. Does not discuss range overlap or how many runs; no results yet.
why: Touches parity protocol design from the adapter-author side but neither critiques nor re-analyses Harbor's criterion.

title: Harbor-Index launch post: 'TERMINAL-BENCH / Harbor-Index' (tbench.ai news, Lin Shi, Haowei Lin, Zixuan Zhu, Xiaoyue Zhou, Xiang Li)
date: 2026 (no day given on page; paper companion is Sept 2026)
summary: Maintainers' announcement of Harbor-Index. States adapters are built for parity and that rigorous parity experiments make the index safe, but reports no parity statistics. What it does report is a native-CLI vs terminus-2 harness comparison per model using paired discordant solve counts with p-values (e.g. GPT-5.5 20/17, p 0.61; Opus 4.8 13/14, p 1; six open models 27/24, p 0.76; Gemini 3.1 10/6, p 0.42), concluding no comparison is significant and differences are within noise at that sample size (~80 pairs each), and that the share of a model's solves surviving a harness swap falls from 42% to 7% as models weaken. Test is not named (counts look like McNemar/sign-test discordant pairs).
why: Shows the maintainers already apply a paired per-task discordant-count significance test to a harness-swap question, which is adjacent to our planned paired per-task parity analysis; however it is applied to native-vs-terminus comparisons, not to adapter parity, and it does not critique range overlap. We should cite it and position our paired analysis as extending their own method to the parity data.

title: How to Measure the Reproducibility of System-oriented IR Experiments (Breuer et al., SIGIR 2020)
summary: Proposes measures to quantify to what extent an IR experiment has been replicated/reproduced, at several granularities (ranked lists, effect sizes, significance outcomes), validated on a reproducibility dataset; implemented in the repro_eval package (arXiv 2201.07599).
why: Prior work on deciding 'when reproduced is reproduced' with graded measures; a template for a per-task parity analysis, though in IR and without TOST.

title: Hugging Face dataset harborframework/parity-experiments — 269 discussion threads (261 are upload PRs); non-PR thread #230 '[Parity] CL-bench: codex/gpt-5.2 ... (50 tasks, 3 trials, MATCHING)'
summary: All 269 discussions scanned; only 8 are non-PR threads and all are result uploads. #230 declares MATCHING on original 6.35 ± 3.26 (runs 2.13, 12.77, 4.17) vs Harbor 8.90 ± 2.98 (runs 8.0, 12.0, 6.52): 'Gap: 2.6pp — within variance on both sides.' No thread contains a statistical re-analysis or criticism of the criterion.
why: Confirms the public per-run data source and that no re-analysis has been posted on the dataset itself; the CL-bench run spread (2-13%) is a vivid example for contribution (2).

title: Inspect Evals docs/methodology.md — guidance for validating a new eval against the paper
summary: Asks contributors to 'Include a small table comparing your results against paper / other frameworks (e.g., model name, score, difference)', 'Document acceptable discrepancies', 'Report uncertainties (e.g. standard error, 95% CI) where feasible', and poses 'How is statistical significance determined?' and 'How many model runs will you perform'. No tolerance, margin, or equivalence test is specified. Last substantive rewrite PR #1568 (2026-05-04); last touched 2026-07-02.
why: The main competing framework's port-validation protocol; relevant comparison point for contribution (3). It stops at CIs/SE and never defines a pass rule, so it does not pre-empt the proposed equivalence protocol.

title: Inspect Evals: docs/methodology.md and 'Developing and Maintaining an Open-Source Repository of AI Evaluations' (arXiv 2507.06893) — ports validated to 'within +/-5% deviation' of reference implementations
summary: Paper: 'Frontier models are run on evaluation subsets to verify that results match reference implementations within +/-5% deviation. Deviations require investigation, which is fairly common.' methodology.md asks contributors to compare aggregate scores to published baselines, document discrepancies, and do repeated runs/paired comparisons where feasible; no numeric tolerance or test named there. Neither uses an equivalence test.
why: Prior art for 'how other harnesses validate ports' (narrows the framing): a fixed ±5% tolerance exists elsewhere, but no statistical equivalence protocol. The paper can position its TOST margin against Inspect's informal 5%.

title: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models
summary: lm-evaluation-harness developers document sensitivity of scores to evaluation setup, difficulty reproducing results reported in papers, and inconsistencies introduced when tasks are adapted across implementations; gives recommendations for rigor.
why: Canonical prior work that re-implementations of the same benchmark diverge; qualitative, with no equivalence testing or error-rate analysis of a matching rule.

title: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models
summary: lm-evaluation-harness maintainers' paper (v3 revised 2026-05-31). Documents that independent implementations of the same benchmark (HELM, lm-eval, original MMLU code) produce widely different scores and change model rankings, that many benchmarks have no ground-truth implementation, and recommends sharing exact prompts/code and reporting uncertainty.
why: Canonical reference that re-implementations of a benchmark do not match the original; it motivates our problem but proposes no statistical criterion for deciding whether two implementations are equivalent.

title: MLPerf Inference Rules (inference_rules.adoc): 99% / 99.9% of reference accuracy and model equivalence to the reference implementation
date: 2026-08-20 (last commit ff7edba); rule dates back to MLPerf Inference v0.5 (paper arXiv 1911.02549, 2019-11-06)
summary: 'All valid submissions of a benchmark must be *equivalent* to the reference implementation.' Closed-division accuracy targets are fixed per benchmark as 99% (or 99.9%) of the FP32/FP16 reference score (e.g. ResNet50 76.46%, Llama3.1-8B rouge, DeepSeek-r1 exact match 81.9132%, GPT-OSS-120B '99% of 83.13%' averaged over 8/5/3 repeats), plus generation-length bands (90-110% of reference tokens). 'Model Equivalence' section defines equivalence via an allowed/disallowed technique list, not a statistical test.
why: The most explicit mature-ecosystem example of a published fixed tolerance for reference-implementation equivalence; needed for the related-work table. Different object (accuracy of a re-implemented model, usually single-run) and no sampling-noise treatment.

title: MLPerf Training Rules: Reference Convergence Points (RCP) checked with a one-sided two-sample t-test at p=0.05
summary: Closed division requires 'same preprocessing, model, training method, and quality target as the reference implementation' and 'mathematical equivalence' with listed exceptions. RCP section: reference is run 2N times; 'Using the mean and standard deviation of the reference convergence we apply a 1-sided independent two-sample Student's t-test with unequal sample sizes, similar variances with p-value=0.05 ... to find the maximum acceptable speedup'; submissions whose mean epochs-to-converge beat the limit are rejected or normalized; failures go through an RCP-bypass audit.
why: A benchmark ecosystem that already uses a formal statistical test with a derived margin to compare a port/submission against a reference distribution; a strong related-work entry that narrows 'first statistical protocol for reference-vs-port' claims. One-sided and about convergence speed, not score equivalence.

title: PaperBench Adapter: parity-validated integration (Harbor PR #408)
summary: Adapter author reports both range-overlap and CI-overlap columns per paper with n=5-9 runs per side. Explicitly notes outliers 'sapg (−0.127, n=5), bam (−0.160, n=6) — both range-overlap-passing' and 'only bbox shows disjoint CIs'. Bot reviews (2026-04/05) recompute SEM and range overlap and flag inconsistencies between reported means and stored run arrays.
why: Contains concrete examples of 13-16 point gaps that pass the overlap rule, and the only in-repo use of CI overlap alongside range overlap; useful evidence, no statistical critique.

title: Porting scBench to inspect_evals (case study with a 'setup parity' test)
summary: Ports LatchBio's scBench (30-task public slice) to inspect_evals. Re-implements five scorer families to upstream tolerances with unit tests, adds test_harness_parity.py comparing prompts/tools/resource settings to the original stack, runs 13 tasks under both setups with Claude Haiku (reported qualitatively: some match, several disagree, two original runs failed to write an answer file). Headline gap: Sonnet 4.5 50.0% in the original mini-SWE-agent setup vs 30.0% under inspect_evals, attributed to harness differences (tool split, Python state persistence, message-limit counting, chat-text-as-answer ~10% inflation, truncation); routing via inspect-swe moved results 'toward parity' without figures. Uses standard errors and Miller (2024) variance components (suggests six repeat batches); 'Declaring a winner among similar models on thirty tasks alone is unreliable.' No TOST, no range-overlap discussion.
why: Prior work that explicitly validates a benchmark port against the original and finds a 20-point harness-induced gap, with SE-based reasoning. Narrows the 'nobody checks ports' framing to 'no one does it with an equivalence test or across many ports'; it is one benchmark, one author, no formal criterion. Cite in related work.

title: Porting scBench to inspect_evals: lessons from running AI agents on single-cell data
summary: Describes an inspect_evals port with a 'setup parity test (test_harness_parity.py)' comparing prompts, tools and resource settings against the original stack, and a per-task pass/fail comparison on 13 shared tasks ('Some tasks matched... Several disagreed') attributed to message limits and truncation; scorers 'follow the same numerical tolerances as upstream'. No tolerance or statistical test for the cross-harness score comparison.
why: An independent port-validation write-up that uses per-task agreement informally; a neighbor for the related-work table, not a competitor.

title: Quantified Reproducibility Assessment of NLP Results (Belz, Popovic, Mille; ACL 2022) and QRA++ (2025)
source: ACL Anthology / arXiv 2204.05961; QRA++ at arXiv 2505.17043 (2025-05-13)
summary: Metrology-based method that turns the gap between an original result and one or more reproductions into a quantified degree-of-reproducibility score (coefficient-of-variation style), tested on 18 system/measure combinations; QRA++ extends to score pairs, rankings and conclusions. Companion: 'A Metrological Perspective on Reproducibility in NLP' (https://aclanthology.org/2022.cl-4.21/).
why: Existing framework for quantifying 'how far is the reproduction from the original', which is adjacent to port parity; it does not use equivalence tests with a margin or address agentic benchmarks.

title: Question About Performance Differences Between Original OpenHands and Harbor-Integrated OpenHands on SWE-Bench Verified (Harbor issue #537)
summary: User asks whether Harbor's OpenHands matches the original on SWE-bench Verified; maintainer li-boxuan: 'We ran parity experiments at a certain point (a few months ago) and the perf diff was negligible'. Closed.
why: Shows users rely on parity claims for port fidelity; no numbers or statistics.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research
summary: Audits 50 agent training/eval repositories (none report failed/errored/skipped runs), documents 37 cases where reporting rules change scores, and shows re-grading preserved outputs under different reporting rules shifts scores by up to 20.9 pp and inverts frontier-model rankings. Proposes rollout cards.
why: Documents that nominally identical benchmarks produce different numbers across implementations and reporting rules (the mechanism behind parity drift), but offers no statistical matching criterion.

title: SafetyRepro: Configuration-Conditional Rank Instability on Alignment Benchmarks
summary: Shows pairwise 'A is safer than B' verdicts depend on under-specified harness configuration; gives a finite-envelope proposition linking a pairwise-disagreement rate to ordering reversals and a commit-stamped protocol. Search snippet reports it re-ran Qwen2.5-7B through lm-evaluation-harness, HELM-lite and Inspect AI with ~22 pp spreads on TruthfulQA/BBQ.
why: Prior work on same-benchmark, different-harness discrepancies across lm-eval-harness/HELM/Inspect (a 'narrowing' item for contribution 2). Abstract page does not name the frameworks or any equivalence test; verify in full text.

title: Shachi: A Modular, Controllable Framework for LLM-Based Agent-Based Modeling of Emergent Collective Behavior
summary: Modular LLM agent-based-modeling framework. Per a search snippet of the full text, the authors use TOST to verify that Shachi's performance distributions are statistically indistinguishable from the original implementations (noting TOST needed N=30 per condition).
why: A documented instance of equivalence testing used to certify a re-implementation matches originals, which is exactly the protocol shape we propose, though for ABM simulations rather than agent benchmarks. The TOST detail is not in the abstract. The full text was read later; see the phase1_verdicts.csv row for arXiv 2509.21862.

title: Terminal-Bench Registry and Adapters announcement ('Tue Jul 15 2025 Release')
summary: First public parity tables for adapted benchmarks (SWE-Bench Verified, AppWorld, DevEval, EvoEval) run with the same agent/model on the original harness and the Terminal-Bench harness; e.g. DevEval 22.8% +/- 4.3 vs 21.6% +/- 3.3 (Claude Code / claude-4-opus). Says adapter rates are 'comparable'; gives no number of runs per side, no definition of the +/- values, and no matching criterion. Lists planned adapters.
why: Primary source for the pre-Harbor parity data and shows the matching criterion was unstated at launch; it is the maintainers' own report, not a re-analysis. Listed for completeness of the timeline.

title: Terminal-Bench: Benchmarking Agents on Hard, Realistic Tasks in Command Line Interfaces
summary: Corrected citation: Mike A. Merrill, Alexander G. Shaw, Nicholas Carlini, Boxuan Li, Harsh Raj, Ivan Bercovich, Lin Shi, Jeong Yeon Shin, Thomas Walshe, E. Kelly Buchanan, Junhong Shen, Guanghao Ye, ... Alex Dimakis, Andy Konwinski, Ludwig Schmidt (85 authors). arXiv:2601.11868, v1 17 Jan 2026 (search results also list it in ICLR 2026 proceedings; not opened). Terminal-Bench 2.0: 89 tasks, frontier agents <65%, error analysis; Section 3.4 describes Harbor as the harness. Appendix D ('Adapters', 26 adapters, Figure 14) says adapters are 'validated via parity experiments' defined as 'controlled comparisons where identical agents and models are evaluated on both the original and adapted versions across multiple trials' that 'ensure that adaptation preserves the benchmark's evaluation semantics'; no pass criterion, run count, or statistics are given. (a) Harbor parity: YES, described qualitatively only. (b) Ports: YES (adapters). (c) Equivalence testing: NO.
why: Directly concerns Harbor adapters and parity experiments but offers no matching criterion or statistical analysis, so it is a primary citation for what parity currently means, not competing work.

title: UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals: CONTRIBUTING.md, EVALUATION_CHECKLIST.md, docs/methodology.md, tools/report_utils.py — port-validation criteria
summary: Criterion is informal similarity, not a test. CONTRIBUTING: 'Comparable - we expect baseline results for at least one frontier model to exist, so we can validate that your implementation produces similar performance'; 'Compare results with reference implementations if available / Document any discrepancies and their causes'. EVALUATION_CHECKLIST: 'A comparison to the original paper is present, or its absence is justified'. methodology.md: 'Run against known reference implementations or published baselines where available and compare aggregate scores; Document acceptable discrepancies (e.g. minor differences due to prompt formatting or randomization); Where feasible, perform repeated runs or paired comparisons across models to estimate uncertainty'; 'Report uncertainties (e.g. standard error, 95% CI) where feasible'. The Evaluation Report tool renders 'Model | Inspect (metric) | Reference | Δ | Samples | Stderr | Time' with Δ = actual - reference and no tolerance. Date given is the v0.23.0 release (PR #2612).
why: Prior practice for validating re-implementations (Inspect Evals ports) — informal, no margin or test. Supports our 'nobody tests equivalence' framing; narrows only if someone had formalised it, which these docs do not.

title: UniACE: A Unified Framework for Evaluating LLM Agentic Capabilities
summary: Migrates 7 existing agent benchmarks (24 domains) into one shared harness, runs 15 models over 400K rollouts, and compares against the source implementations, reporting 'large bidirectional score changes' (e.g. tens of points on AgentBench/tau2-bench) and model-ranking reversals.
why: A systematic re-implementation study showing ported benchmarks often do not match the original: narrows our 'does a port match?' framing. Abstract gives no parity criterion or equivalence test. The full text was read later; see the phase1_verdicts.csv row for arXiv 2605.27898.

title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
summary: Runs 5 models through 3 agent harnesses (Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, OpenCode) on SWE-bench Verified (447 tasks; 45-task hard subset), orchestrated through Harbor. Pairs task outcomes across harnesses, tests gaps with exact McNemar + Newcombe interval, uses rerun spread as the noise yardstick, reports the smallest gap detectable at 80% power ('45 tasks catch a 13-point gap only half the time... 447 tasks resolve 5 points'), and on the 447-task pool runs an explicit TOST equivalence test at delta = 5 points (pass if 90% interval inside +/-delta).
why: Uses exactly the statistical toolkit we propose (paired per-task McNemar, TOST with stated margin, power/run-count calculation, Harbor-orchestrated runs) on an agentic benchmark. 'Harness' here means agent scaffold, not a benchmark port; it does not analyse parity experiments or the range-overlap rule, so it narrows the methodological novelty of contribution (3) rather than killing anything.

title: What Does an Evaluation License? A Commit-Bound Census of Claim Replay in Inspect Evals
summary: Freezes the Inspect Evals collection at a commit (124 eligible units) and attempts to replay its historical claims; most units stop because the evidence needed for replay is not bound; where replay works, claims are stable at different resolutions.
why: Systematic audit of a re-implemented evaluation collection's claims; no statistical equivalence criterion visible in the abstract, but it is the closest 'can a ported eval support its claims' study outside Harbor.

title: What Does an Evaluation License? A Commit-Bound Census of Claim Replay in Inspect Evals
summary: Freezes the Inspect Evals collection at a commit and attempts to replay the historical claims (reported results) of its ported evaluations; finds most units cannot be replayed because the required evidence is not bound, and where replay works, claims are stable only at certain resolutions. Ancillary files mention independent recomputation and cross-checks.
why: A systematic study of whether a port collection (Inspect Evals) reproduces original claims, which is the port-versus-original question. Abstract does not mention statistical or equivalence tests. The full text was read later; see the phase1_verdicts.csv row for arXiv 2608.19269.

title: What Does an Evaluation License? A Commit-Bound Census of Claim Replay in Inspect Evals (arXiv 2608.19269)
summary: Qin & Tong freeze the Inspect Evals collection and attempt to replay its historical claims (published reference values); 'Most units stop because the evidence required for replay is not bound. Where replay is possible, different claims remain stable at different resolutions.' Ancillary files include INDEPENDENT_RECOMPUTATION.json and a pytrec_eval cross-check. v4 revised 2026-08-29. Abstract does not mention equivalence testing, TOST, tolerance, or CIs.
why: Closest prior work to 'systematic study of whether re-implemented benchmarks match the original' (for Inspect Evals rather than Harbor). Narrows the novelty of contribution (2)'s framing; does not use equivalence tests and does not touch Harbor.

title: What's going on with the Open LLM Leaderboard? (Fourrier, Habib, Launay, Wolf)
summary: Compares MMLU under three implementations (original, HELM, lm-eval-harness) for 8 models: llama-65b scores 0.636 / 0.637 / 0.488, i.e. a ~15-point gap for identical weights, caused by prompt-format and answer-scoring differences; rankings also change. No statistical test or criterion for implementation equivalence is proposed.
why: The most-cited concrete demonstration that a port can silently become a different benchmark; a direct motivating example for us, but descriptive only.

title: When LLMs get significantly worse: A statistical approach to detect model degradations
summary: Hypothesis-testing framework (McNemar, per-sample paired comparison, controlled false-positive rate) implemented on lm-evaluation-harness to decide whether an optimized/quantized model variant has degraded; aggregates across benchmarks; attributes drops as small as 0.3% to real degradation while not flagging provably lossless optimizations.
why: Same 'is variant B still the same as A' question with paired per-item tests on a standard harness; framed as degradation detection, not equivalence with a margin, and not about ports.

title: When Top-k Truncation Is Not the Bottleneck: An Equivalence-Test Audit of LLM Logprob Calibration
summary: Argues equivalence claims in LLM evaluation need TOST with pre-specified margins and paired-bootstrap inference rather than failed significance tests; applies it to top-k logprob truncation and other pipeline configuration changes, reporting equivalence at delta_ECE=0.02 in some settings and inconclusive pre-registered results on GPQA Diamond (n=198).
why: Closest methodological precedent for 'use TOST, state a margin, report inconclusive' in LLM evaluation. Does not address benchmark ports, harnesses or parity (confirmed on the venue page).

title: [Deferred][Score] SWE-Bench Verified matched-config paired run (ca-mrc/loom issue #20)
summary: A third-party harness (Loom) plans to validate its SWE-bench Verified implementation against Harbor's published 54.5 ± 0.7 (mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 + gpt-5-mini, 3 runs, same 499-task subset) and classify 'paired_validated' if the difference is <= 2 percentage points, else 'paired_delta_flagged'. Never run (no API keys; closed 2026-07-29 as duplicate of #32).
why: Independent use of a fixed 2-pp margin for port validation against Harbor numbers — a crude precursor to an equivalence margin; not a test, not executed, not a critique of Harbor's rule.

title: [Doc] Split adapter tutorial to human/ai (harbor PR #1403) — introduces 'match if and only if run-score ranges overlap' plus a per-task debug playbook
summary: Commit 9ad34d5f added to docs/content/docs/datasets/adapters.mdx the 'Matching criterion' section (max(A)>=min(B) AND max(B)>=min(A); 'Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match') and a 'Debug playbook' whose step 3 is 'Overlap analysis: per-task resolution on each side; list tasks resolved on A-only and on B-only. A roughly symmetric split suggests sampling noise; a lopsided split suggests systematic adaptation error' and step 4 'Distinguish randomness from systematic error' by whether disagreements persist across runs. title: harbor-framework/harbor PR #1387 "Adapter: Frontier-CS" review thread (bot + maintainers applying the range-overlap rule)

The reviewer bot flags, in passing, exactly the failure modes we plan to formalise: Problem 14 original runs [95.32, 95.42, 95.65] vs Harbor [34.11, 45.0, 96.04] is called 'technically overlaps but the harbor mean is ~37 points below the original'; Problem 13 [33.08,33.08] vs [2.81] 'no range overlap'; after zeros from token-limit failures are included on both sides, 'all 10 entries pass range overlap' because both ranges become [0, max]. This is not a critique paper and does not kill our contribution 1, but it must be cited: it shows the weakness is visible in the record, and a reviewer could say 'the maintainers already know'.

title: harbor-framework/harbor PR #1654 "Adapter: asta-bench" review thread (17/22 cells pass overlap; zero-minimum cells 'trivially' overlap)
summary: PR body states the criterion explicitly ('ranges overlap (max Upstream = 25.67 >= min Harbor = 18.82 ...)', 'Sample SEM = sqrt(sum/(n(n-1))) with n=3', solver at temperature=1 so 'cross-run variance on both sides reflects agent stochasticity'). Bot reviews recount a per-family range-overlap matrix (first 15/22, corrected to 17/22) and note that two cells pass only because 'both sides share a minimum of 0.0, so the ranges trivially overlap'; one cell where Harbor outscored the original with no overlap is called 'unusual and unexplained'. Eventually the per-family breakdown is removed from the JSON and only the OVERALL metric (which overlaps) is kept, so the adapter 'satisfies the matching criterion'.
why: Documents the rule being gamed by aggregation level (per-family fails, overall passes) and by zero-floors. Supports our claim that the rule is weak, and should be cited as an observed case rather than re-derived. No one in the thread proposes CIs, TOST or paired tests.

title: harbor-framework/harbor PR #1836 "Adapter: OsWorld" review thread (n=1 per side; rule 'can't be formally satisfied')
summary: Full-suite parity is one run per side (0.4026 vs 0.4226). Bot: 'Parity is n=1 per side, so the range-overlap criterion can't be formally satisfied... single points, no overlap, SEM undefined... Means are reassuringly close (~2% absolute)'. A 6-run subset ([0.4,0.5,0.3,0.4,0.7,0.5] vs [0.4,0.5,0.6,0.3,0.6,0.7]) is accepted because ranges [0.3,0.7] 'overlap'.

title: harbor-framework/harbor PR #728 "Adapter: CL-Bench" review thread (reviewer invokes confidence intervals and 'statistical significance' informally)
summary: On an n=1 parity (20.0% vs 14.3%) the bot writes 'A single run gives no statistical measure of variability... Running 3+ times per side would give error bars and strengthen the equivalence claim' and 'Most accepted adapters run at least 3 trials per side'. On a later ~9pp gap: 'The confidence intervals barely overlap... This is a statistically significant gap, not within normal variance... The PR should not claim parity'. Maintainer jweihe counters that '~6pp gap is within expected variance for LLM-as-judge benchmarks at this sample size'. Final accepted parity: original [0.10,0.14,0.12] vs harbor [0.12,0.08,0.12], 'range overlap [10-12%] satisfies Harbor range-overlap parity criterion'.
why: Closest thing found to a statistical argument about a parity result inside the Harbor process: informal CI-overlap reasoning and a 'within expected variance' claim with no test. Confirms no one has run a proper equivalence analysis, while showing the vocabulary (CI, significance, equivalence claim) is already in play. Cite as motivation.

No further mention of the study anywhere in comments, reviews, or commits; the most likely output is the parity appendix (D.4/D.7) of arXiv 2609.04298, covered in its own rows.

title: tbench.ai news: 'Harbor-Index' (harness comparison reports 'No comparison reaches a significant winner (all p > 0.05)', 'within noise at this sample size')
date: 2026-06-29 (news index date); page by Lin Shi, Haowei Lin, Zixuan Zhu, Xiaoyue Zhou, Xiang Li
summary: Native harness vs Terminus-2 on ~80 task pairs per model; p-values 0.61, 1, 0.76, 0.42 with the test unnamed; concludes differences are 'within noise'. Says 'Rigorous parity experiments are what make it safe to curate Harbor-Index' but presents no parity statistics.
