title: A Monte Carlo Study Comparing Various Two-Sample Tests for Differences in Mean
summary: Neave & Granger compare eight two-sample tests (including Tukey's quick test and Neave's quick test) by simulation at n=20 and n=40, normal and bimodal; Normal Scores test best overall, Neave's the best quick test. Only one 2023+ citer in OpenAlex/S2 (a 2023 JDSSV paper on whether to test model assumptions first); nothing in ML.
why: Statistical prior art on the power of quick tests, needed to cite; does not study n=3 and has no benchmark application.

title: A Monte-Carlo Study of Type I Error Rates and Power for Tukey's Pocket Test
source: The Journal of General Psychology 123(4):333-339 (Dunlap, Greer & Beatty)
summary: Extends Neave & Granger with simulations of Tukey's pocket test for sample sizes 5 to 100, normal and skewed; reports Tukey's critical values hold up even under heavy skew. Only 2 citations in OpenAlex.
why: The only dedicated power study of the test found; its smallest n is 5, so the n=3 impossibility result (max end count 6) is outside its range and is not stated there. Cite as context.

title: A Quick, Compact, Two-Sample Test to Duckworth's Specifications
summary: Tukey's end-count ('pocket'/'quick') two-sample test: count values in one sample beyond all of the other plus the reverse; critical totals roughly 7, 10, 13 for two-sided 5%, 1%, 0.1% (confirmed on the Wikipedia page, which cites only this paper). OpenAlex lists two records (W4233114005, 70 cites; W1985407020, 119 cites). Forward citations 2023-2026: 7 in OpenAlex (reliability engineering, quality engineering, fungi, agronomy, pharmacology, two multivariate two-sample-test papers), 1 in Semantic Scholar; none in ML/LLM/benchmarking.
why: Must-cite original for the degenerate-Tukey-test argument (two groups of 3 cap the end count at 6 < 7). No 2023-2026 citer applies it to benchmarks, leaderboards or ports, so the framing is not pre-empted.

title: A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning: Pitfalls and Paths to Reproducibility
summary: Shows reasoning-benchmark results are highly sensitive to decoding parameters, seeds, prompt formatting, hardware and software configuration; proposes a standardized evaluation framework and reporting standards.
why: Implementation-sensitivity neighbor; not ports or equivalence.

title: AI Achieves a Perfect LSAT Score
summary: Per search snippet: applies TOST with a +/-2 pp margin and notes the N=77 sample is too small to support that margin, so only significance tests are reported.
why: TOST-in-LLM-eval precedent that explicitly reports underpowered equivalence; snippet only.

title: AI Agents That Matter
summary: Corrected citation: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, Arvind Narayanan. arXiv:2407.01502, v1 1 Jul 2024. Argues agent evals over-focus on accuracy, conflate model vs downstream developer needs, lack holdouts, and lack standardization/reproducibility; reports reproduction attempts on HumanEval/WebArena where many published accuracies exceed the max of five of their own runs, and notes agent developers often must re-implement benchmark evaluation scripts. (a) Harbor parity: NO. (b) Ports/re-implementations: only in passing (re-implementing eval scripts causes inconsistencies; no systematic study). (c) Equivalence testing: NO.
why: Reproducibility neighbor; motivates why ports drift but provides no port-vs-original comparison method or statistics.

title: AdaStop: adaptive statistical testing for sound comparisons of Deep RL agents
summary: Group-sequential multiple test to decide how many independent executions are needed to compare RL algorithms; states that fewer than 5 executions 'is not enough in general'. Cites Cumming & Finch 2005 (found via S2 citation list).
why: Statistical prior art on run counts for noisy agent comparisons; not about ports or equivalence margins.

title: Adaptation Fidelity of SPEC CPU2026 (arXiv 2608.27710)
summary: Systematically compares SPEC CPU2026 benchmarks against their upstream open-source applications under official inputs in single-copy and 192-copy runs; most match closely, some outliers from SPEC's adaptation (I/O reduction). Search snippet also mentions SPEC harness validation against golden reference outputs 'within the specified tolerances for each benchmark' (not in abstract).
why: A systematic 'does the adapted benchmark match the original' study in a non-ML ecosystem; neighbor for the related-work table.

title: Add automated adapter review bot for PR validation (harbor PR #857) — first codified overlap check
summary: Initial review bot (Zixuan Zhu / Ternura143). adapter-review.yml prompt asked: 'Do the parity scores (mean ± std) show obvious overlaps that demonstrate equivalence?' Slimshilin's review requested: 'The scores mean +- std should have obvious overlaps to show equival[ence]' and 'individual trial scores, task overlap / failure analysis'. No statistical discussion. Later versions: PR #1023 (2026-03-08) 'Parity scores (mean ± std) show overlap demonstrating equivalence'; PR #1399 (2026-04-09) added a check that asymmetric run counts be explained in notes.
why: Documents the lineage of the rule (mean±std overlap -> range overlap). No critique or statistical proposal in any historical version of adapter_review.py or adapter-review.yml.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
summary: Corrected citation: Evan Miller (Anthropic). arXiv:2411.00640 [stat.AP], v1 1 Nov 2024, 14 pages. Treats eval questions as a sample from a super-population; gives CLT standard errors, clustered SEs (can be >3x naive), variance reduction by resampling (K attempts per question) and next-token probabilities, paired analysis of question-level differences when comparing two models, and a power/sample-size formula with a Minimum Detectable Effect. (a) Harbor parity: NO. (b) Ports/re-implementations: NO. (c) Equivalence testing: NO (frequentist difference tests only; 'equivalent' appears only in the clustered-SE derivation). Notes Inspect's built-in stderr() metric.
why: General eval-statistics neighbor; it is the natural methodological base for the SEM, paired per-task and sample-size parts of our protocol, but contains no equivalence (TOST) framing and nothing about ports or parity.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
summary: Evan Miller's note treating evals as experiments: super-population framing, formulas for standard errors, two-model comparisons (paired differences) and evaluation planning.
why: Standard reference for CIs and paired comparisons in evals; no equivalence testing or ports.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
summary: Recommends CLT standard errors, clustered SEs, variance reduction by resampling, paired question-level differences for model comparisons, and power analysis. Verified on the HTML: does not discuss the overlap heuristic, does not cite Schenker/Payton/Cumming/Belia, no TOST/non-inferiority, no re-implementations or harness differences (only notes Llama 3 mis-estimates SEs and Inspect computes them correctly).
why: Known eval-noise neighbor; checked specifically for whether the CI-overlap literature had been imported into LLM evals; this paper does not import it.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations (Evan Miller, arXiv 2411.00640)
summary: Clustered standard errors, paired-difference variance reduction, power analysis for evals. No ports or equivalence testing.
why: Standard neighbor; foundation for paired per-task CIs.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations (Miller)
summary: Recommends CLT-based confidence intervals, paired differences, clustered standard errors and power analysis for LLM evals.
why: Error-bar neighbor; our CI/paired analysis builds on it but it does not consider ports or equivalence.

title: Advanced AI evaluations at AISI: May update
summary: Compares AISI's GAIA scaffold (25%) to published scaffolds (FRIDAY 24%, MAE 32%) 'to independently verify that our scaffold provided the models with support that is close to the state-of-the-art'; grader vs human Cohen's kappa 0.52; 5-10 runs per task; no error bars, no tolerance.
why: Only AISI post found on validating an implementation against published numbers; no protocol. No AISI blog titled around 'validating evals' was found.

title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard
summary: Corrected citation: Michael Hardy, Ruhana Azam, Anka Reuel, Mykel Kochenderfer, Sanmi Koyejo. arXiv:2610.00651 [v1, 30 Sep 2026]. Bayesian variance-decomposition (generalizability theory) applied to 30,859 rollouts from 9 HAL benchmarks and 13 Harbor-Index benchmarks (22 total). Finds fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994) but underlying-model reliability is much lower (0.148-0.841); scaffold choice can flip conclusions; adding tasks raises model-ranking reliability by at most ~0.097 when scaffold coverage is the bottleneck; pooling benchmarks helps. (a) Harbor parity: NO. Harbor appears only as a data source (Harbor-Index task-level scores, 9 LLMs x 4 scaffolds) and as a citation of arXiv 2609.04298 v3; the one 'parity' hit is unrelated ('structural parity'). (b) Ports/re-implementations: NO. (c) Equivalence testing: NO (only 'equivalently' in math).
why: Closest eval-noise neighbor because it works on Harbor-Index data and decomposes run variance, but its question is ranking reliability across tasks/scaffolds, not whether a Harbor port matches its original. Must cite and distinguish; no overlap with contributions 1-3.

title: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard (arXiv 2610.00651)
summary: Hardy, Azam, Reuel, Kochenderfer, Koyejo. Bayesian G-theory variance decomposition on 22 benchmarks from HAL and the Harbor Index (used as a supplemental meta-dataset: 29 benchmarks, 9 LLMs, 4 scaffolds). Finds model-scaffold systems rank reliably (Eρ² 0.935-0.994) but underlying models do not (0.148-0.841); scaffold choice can flip conclusions; more tasks cannot fix scaffold-driven uncertainty. Full-text search: no 'parity', 'adapter' (except in the Harbor reference), 'TOST', or 'equivalence'. Cites 2609.04298.
why: Citing work and the strongest eval-noise neighbor using Harbor data; does not examine original-vs-port fidelity or runs-per-side.

title: Agent evals with Harbor (Jeff Linwood blog; AIMUG talk 'Harbor evals for coding agents')
source: jefflinwood.com + YouTube (Austin AI MUG); talk transcript
summary: Practitioner uses Harbor to run 120 sandboxed trials (two repetitions per condition) testing instruction styles for MCP tool use; concludes the sample is too small for agent- or model-specific conclusions. No adapters, parity or statistical tests.
why: Community Harbor usage with an explicit too-few-runs caveat; not about ports.

title: AgentBeats: Agentifying Agent Assessment for Openness, Standardization, and Reproducibility

why: Harness-discrepancy neighbour in the Terminal-Bench ecosystem; snippet only.

title: Agents Are Systems, Not Models: Rethinking Agentic Evaluation
summary: Studies five agent configuration choices on four scientific tasks; ~54% of outcome variance comes from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it; releases 18,000+ trajectories.
why: Eval-noise neighbour quantifying run-to-run variance share.

title: AlgoPerf (mlcommons/algorithmic-efficiency) JAX-vs-PyTorch workload diff tests
summary: test_traindiffs.py trains both framework implementations for NUM_TRAIN_STEPS and asserts numpy.allclose on eval metric, grad norm and loss with rtol=1 (i.e. 100% relative tolerance); tests/modeldiffs/diff.py converts PyTorch weights to JAX and prints max/min forward-pass difference without asserting. The paper's text contains no equivalence requirement or tolerance; Author Contributions only say 'Developed test suites to compare the implementations of workloads across frameworks that caught several implementation deficiencies'.
why: Example of 'framework parity' testing with a very loose stated tolerance; useful as a related-work row, not a competitor.

title: Anytime-Valid LLM Leaderboards via Benchmark-weighted and Block-Factorized e-Processes
summary: BB-EDGE: e-process based certification of pairwise mean-performance advantages with anytime FWER control, motivated by run-to-run variability producing unsupported superiority claims.
why: Neighbor on leaderboard reliability under run variability; no ports/parity.

title: Anytime-Valid LLM Leaderboards via Benchmark-weighted and Block-Factorized e-Processes
summary: BB-EDGE: e-process framework certifying pairwise mean-performance advantages on leaderboards with anytime-valid FWER control, motivated by run-to-run variability producing unsupported superiority claims.
why: Leaderboard-noise neighbour; not ports/parity.

title: Applying Statistics to LLM Evaluations
summary: Practitioner tutorial built on Miller 2024. States 'overlapping intervals do not by themselves rule [a difference] out', that non-overlap implies significance, and that 'checking overlap of separate confidence intervals is conservative' / 'overly conservative for detecting performance differences'. Gives no citation for those claims. No TOST, no ports, no analysis of running a whole benchmark 3 times (its K=3 is per-question resampling).
why: Shows the 'overlap is conservative' point is already in LLM-eval folklore (without citing Schenker/Payton); contribution (1) should be framed as quantifying the specific range-overlap-at-k=3 rule rather than as discovering that overlap tests are weak.

title: Artificial Analysis — Intelligence Benchmarking Methodology (Index v4.3.2)
summary: Per-eval repeats of 1, 3 or 5 (e.g. Terminal-Bench 4.0 'pass@1 scoring averaged over 3 repeats per task'); sandwich-estimator 95% CIs for Elo-style evals; several 'scores are not directly comparable' caveats across versions/providers. No stated tolerance or rule for agreement with lab-reported scores (only the first part of this long page was read).
why: Independent evaluator; no port-validation rule; context only.

Reviewer asked to 'Put mean and std of one side together ... leave the individual run scores as columns' and the author replied 'we may build a parity dashboard on harbor-docs. Will track as a follow-up'. No analysis beyond tabulation.

title: Automated Benchmark Auditing for AI Agents and Large Language Models
summary: Agentic auditor (ABA) over 168 benchmarks finds issues in 25.7% of tasks; filtering shifts rankings and raises Terminal-Bench 2 scores by 9.6%.
why: Task-validity neighbour on the same benchmarks; not about ports.

title: BDD-Bench: A Behavior-Driven Benchmark for Coding Agents across the Application Lifecycle
summary: 111 repository-level Gherkin-spec instances; thirteen models 'under a single agent harness with three runs each'; introduces a failure taxonomy and 'a matched-rerun des[ign]' (abstract truncated in OpenAlex). No ports or parity.
why: One of only two OpenAlex-recorded citers of the Terminal-Bench paper; repeated-run design but not port parity.

title: Bayesian Data Analysis in Empirical Software Engineering Research (Furia, Feldt, Torkar)
summary: Advocates Bayesian analysis (posterior intervals, practical-significance regions) over NHST in empirical SE, with reanalyses of published experiments.
why: ROPE-style practical-equivalence reasoning in SE; neighbor for the equivalence-testing literature.

title: Benchmark Drift: silent revisions of Hugging Face benchmark evaluation splits (data and code)
source: Zenodo (Sahay, Tiwari, Gupta; submitted to IEEE Access)

Compares across dataset revisions, not across harness ports; no statistical tests described.
why: Neighbour on 'is it still the same benchmark' from the data-revision side rather than the harness-port side.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
summary: Audits 4 tool-calling benchmark families; 18.5% evaluator-human misalignment; in LiveMCPBench 23 repeated runs of the same setup scored 57.9%-76.8%; releases Harness Lab for repeated-run comparison.
why: Documents run-to-run spread large enough to swamp any 3-run parity comparison; not about ports.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
summary: From the search-result snippet only: re-ran a 95-task LiveMCPBench configuration 23 times and found scores ranging 57.9% to 76.8% (SD 5.4 points), concluding single-run scores cannot support fine-grained comparisons. Not opened.
why: Agent-benchmark run-to-run noise neighbor that supports the 'k=3 ranges are wide' argument; not about ports or overlap rules. Title only; not opened.

title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
summary: Benchmark-quality assessment framework (46 criteria) applied to 24 benchmarks; reproducibility and statistical reporting are among the criteria.
why: Benchmark-quality neighbor.

title: Beyond Point Estimates: Reliable Evaluation of Prediction Performance Metrics under Clustered Data
summary: Cluster-robust sandwich variance for confusion-matrix metrics giving CIs, paired model comparisons, and power/sample-size approximations; search snippet frames candidate-vs-reference non-inferiority.
why: Statistical-methods neighbour for paired comparison and power; no benchmark ports.

title: Bluesky mirror of Theo's post comparing Artificial Analysis vs Harbor Hub Terminal-Bench numbers
summary: Notes that Harbor Hub ran models with the official harness and that all models score higher there than on Artificial Analysis, with the largest bump for one model when moving from mini-swe-agent to codex. A leaderboard-discrepancy-by-harness observation; no parity or adapter content.
why: Only substantive Bluesky hit; harness-discrepancy neighbour, not a parity analysis.

title: Can We Hide Machines in the Crowd? Quantifying Equivalence in LLM-in-the-loop Annotation Tasks
summary: Per search snippet: TOST to test whether replacing a human annotator with an LLM keeps agreement within a margin derived from natural variation among human annotators.
why: Precedent for deriving the equivalence margin from natural variation (analogous to deriving a parity margin from run-to-run noise); snippet only.

title: Can We Hide Machines in the Crowd? Quantifying Equivalence in LLM-in-the-loop Annotation Tasks
summary: Combines Krippendorff's alpha, paired bootstrapping and TOST to test whether an LLM annotator is statistically equivalent to human annotators (passes on MovieLens, p=0.004; fails on PolitiFact, p=0.155).
why: TOST applied in an LLM evaluation context; unrelated to benchmark ports.

title: Can We Hide Machines in the Crowd? Quantifying Equivalence in LLM-in-the-loop Annotation Tasks (arXiv 2510.06658)
summary: He et al. use Krippendorff's α, paired bootstrapping and TOST to test whether an LLM annotator is statistically equivalent to human annotators (MovieLens 100K p=0.004; PolitiFact p=0.155). Not about benchmark re-implementations.
why: Only LLM-eval paper found using TOST; useful as methodological precedent, no overlap with ports.

title: ClawBenchPro: Benchmarking How Well Agent Harnesses Work
summary: 1.0k-sample, 43-domain benchmark run across 14 LLMs and four agent harnesses; reports harness-dependent score differences (3.2-6.5% accuracy trade-off between harnesses) but no parity/equivalence methodology.
why: Harness-comparison neighbor; does not test whether a benchmark survives a port.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
summary: Observational audit of 254 SWE-bench submissions; exact paired McNemar separates none of the 29 adjacent Verified top-30 pairs; explicitly notes that non-rejection does not establish equivalence and that no practical-equivalence margin is specified; estimates the instance budget needed for resolution.
why: Neighbor: paired per-instance tests on an agentic benchmark and an explicit acknowledgement of the equivalence gap we fill; not about ports.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
summary: Audits 254 SWE-bench submissions without reruns. Top two Verified entries each resolve 396/500; most adjacent top-30 comparisons are not separated by exact paired McNemar tests with Holm correction; scores depend on the model-scaffold pair; proposes a three-tier grouping, a five-step audit protocol and reporting of model-scaffold provenance. Explicitly cautions that 'non-rejection does not establish equivalence' but does not run an equivalence test (no TOST), and does not discuss ports, adapters or parity experiments.
why: Methodological neighbour for contribution 3: uses per-instance paired exact tests on public per-task results and makes the non-rejection-vs-equivalence point. Not about ports or Harbor; our paired analysis across original-vs-port is distinct, but we should cite it and use the same McNemar machinery.

title: Comparing the Results of Replications in Software Engineering
summary: Analyses a series of SE experiment replications where equality-of-means could never be rejected yet effect sizes appeared to conflict; discusses how to compare replication results.
why: Illustrates in ESE that failing to find a difference is not evidence of equivalence; general neighbor for the equivalence-testing literature.

title: Computer Use at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice
summary: Shows a replay script beats frontier CUAs on static benchmarks; proposes PRISM environment principles and DigiWorld, plus an aggregation framework pairing Wilson score intervals with a hierarchical bootstrap over scenarios, configuration axes and rollouts (R=20; Wilson near-nominal down to R=3). No ports, re-implementations, Harbor, parity, TOST or two-setup equivalence tests.
why: Eval-noise neighbor: a published argument that naive aggregation and small-R intervals mislead in agent benchmarks, useful for motivating CIs on k=3 parity runs; it does not address matching two harnesses.

title: Consistency as a Testable Property: Statistical Methods to Evaluate AI Agent Reliability
summary: U-statistics for output-level reliability and kernel metrics for trajectory-level stability under semantics-preserving perturbations, evaluated on three agentic benchmarks; argues trajectory consistency is more diagnostic than pass@1.
why: Statistical-methods-for-agent-eval neighbor; not about ports, parity or equivalence of two harnesses.

title: Converted, Not Equivalent: Benchmarking Codebase Conversion via Observational Equivalence
summary: T2J-Bench: fixed verifier checks source vs converted codebases in Spec/Numeric/Behavioral stages; agents overestimate conversion success by 66-98 points.
why: 'Port equivalence' by analogy (code conversion), not benchmark evaluation parity.

title: Converted, Not Equivalent: Benchmarking Codebase Conversion via Observational Equivalence (T2J-Bench; arXiv 2605.29054)
summary: Treats PyTorch-to-JAX codebase conversion as transfer under a 'fixed equivalence contract' verified in three stages (interface Spec; Numeric agreement on outputs/losses/gradients within tolerance budgets per precision profile; Behavioral short-training dynamics under fixed seeds). Agents overestimate success by 66.6-97.8 points relative to the fixed verifier.
why: Tolerance-based equivalence for ports of code, not benchmarks/evals; a related-work row on 'ports validated by stated tolerance'.

title: Crossing the Validation Crisis: Cross-Validation Reduces Benchmarking Variance Surprisingly Well

why: General benchmarking-variance neighbour.

title: Crossing the Validation Crisis: Cross-Validation Reduces Benchmarking Variance Surprisingly Well
summary: Introduces 'sample gain' to quantify variance reduction from multiple CV splits when benchmarking learning algorithms; early-stopping rule for folds. Classic ML benchmarking, not LLM agent harnesses.
why: General eval-variance neighbor only.

title: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks

why: Documents the run-to-run-interval convention used in the Harbor/Terminal-Bench ecosystem and its blind spot to task sampling; no parity analysis.

title: DeltaSelect: Affordable A/B Testing for Coding Agents
summary: Selects a fixed task subset whose single-run results track full-benchmark performance (Pearson correlation on DeepSWE trials) for cheap repeated baseline-vs-candidate comparisons of coding agents. No equivalence testing, run-count analysis, Harbor or ports.
why: Paired baseline-vs-candidate comparison neighbour; not about port parity.

title: Deployment Decision Reliability: A Generalizability-Theory Framework for Sizing Long-Horizon Agent Evaluations (arXiv 2608.11323)
summary: Srinivasan. G-theory decomposition on TheAgentCompany, τ²-bench, AppWorld: agent main effect <3% of variance, agent×task 7-23%; proposes a 'Deployment Decision Reliability' reporting discipline. No ports, parity, or equivalence testing; no explicit runs-per-side recommendation in the abstract.
why: Neighbor on sizing evaluations; relevant to contribution (3)'s 'runs needed' only as related work.

title: Disclosure-Gated User Simulation for Companion-Agent Evaluation

why: Example of TOST-style three-way verdicts in agent evaluation; not ports. Snippet only.

Taxonomy of eight reward-hacking flaw patterns, an 'Agent-Eval Checklist', and BenchJack, an automated red-teaming system applied to 10 agent benchmarks (219 flaws; near-perfect scores without solving tasks) plus an iterative patch loop. Harbor is mentioned only as the coordinator of FrontierSWE whose reward files an agent can pre-write. (a) Harbor parity: NO. (b) Ports/re-implementations: NO. (c) Equivalence testing: NO.

title: Do These LLM Benchmarks Agree? Fixing Benchmark Evaluation with BenchBench
summary: Benchmark Agreement Testing across 40+ benchmarks; shows methodological choices change agreement conclusions; releases BenchBench.
why: Agreement between different benchmarks, not between a benchmark and its port.

title: Efficient Evaluation of LLM Performance with Statistical Guarantees
summary: Casts benchmarking as finite-population inference; Factorized Active Querying gives valid frequentist CIs for accuracy under a query budget, up to 5x effective-sample-size gains.
why: CI-construction neighbor; no ports or equivalence testing.

summary: Checklist: 'Is the task an existing benchmark in the literature? Have you referenced the original paper that introduced the task? No numerical parity requirement anywhere. Date is the access date (live files).

title: Equivalence Tests: A Practical Primer for t Tests, Correlations, and Meta-Analyses (Lakens 2017)

title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Corrected citation: Yuxuan Zhu, Tengjun Jin, Yada Pruksachatkun, Andy Zhang, Shu Liu, Sasha Cui, Sayash Kapoor, Shayne Longpre, Kevin Meng, Rebecca Weiss, Fazl Barez, Rahul Gupta, ... title: HF dataset harborframework/parity-experiments discussions #210 and #230 - CL-bench parity, non-matching then 'MATCHING' at 2.6pp gap

summary: Frames paired LLM leaderboard comparisons as hypothesis tests, inverts level/power to get required N*, reports resolution ratio q=N/N*; finds many displayed pairwise rankings on Open LLM Leaderboard v1 and MMLU-Pro are unresolved at (0.05, 0.8), and that the unpaired Cohen-h shortcut is off by ~2x in the close-comparison regime.
why: Leaderboard-reliability neighbor with a sample-size calculation; no ports, no equivalence margin, no range overlap.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research
summary: Audit of 50 agent repos (none report failed/errored/skipped runs); 37 cases where reporting rules change success rates; re-grading preserved rollouts shows changing only the reporting rule shifts scores by up to 20.9 points and can reverse rankings; proposes 'rollout cards'.
why: Shows harness/reporting choices alone move agent scores by tens of points (a mechanism behind port drift); no parity or equivalence analysis.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research (arXiv 2605.12131)
summary: Audit of 50 repos; re-grading preserved outputs under different reporting rules shifts scores by up to 20.9pp and can invert rankings. Reporting standard, not port validation.
why: Neighbor; relevant to how errored/skipped trials are counted in parity runs.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research (arXiv 2605.12131)
summary: Audits 50 agent repos (none report failed/errored/skipped runs), identifies 37 reporting-rule choices that change scores; re-grading preserved outputs shifts scores up to 20.9 pp and flips rankings; proposes 'rollout cards'. No port validation or tolerance.
why: Agent-eval reproducibility neighbor; relevant to why parity records need per-task/per-trial data.

title: SCLATE: A Substrate for Continual-Learning Agent Training and Evaluation (arXiv 2609.32391)
summary: Jung et al. Event-scheduler substrate with simulated clock; 'We port seven benchmarks to SCLATE and compare ten unmodified harness and memory configurations'. Cites 2609.04298 (per search) for benchmark limitations; abstract reports no parity or equivalence check for its ports.

title: SafeLLM4SE: Statistical Evaluation and Reporting for LLM-based Software Engineering Systems
summary: Methodology and reporting standard treating LLM outputs as a stochastic process: adaptive sampling with confidence intervals, distribution-aware comparisons, effect sizes, minimum reporting standard; PyPI package; illustrated on HumanEval. Full text has no equivalence test, TOST, parity, port or Harbor mentions.
why: General eval-statistics neighbour for software-engineering LLM evaluation; could be cited for CI/reporting practice.

title: SafetyRepro: Configuration-Conditional Rank Instability on Alignment Benchmarks (arXiv 2605.25492)
summary: Shows that changing evaluation configuration/harness alone can flip pairwise model verdicts on every alignment benchmark tested; proposes a commit-stamped protocol. No Harbor, parity, or equivalence testing.
why: Neighbor on harness-induced score differences; not about ports or equivalence.

title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
summary: Sydney Lewis. Compares two configurations of one harness (full transcript vs context-compaction treatment) on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and FeatureBench with model and tasks fixed; under tight context the treatment raises mean fail-to-pass from 28% to 49% (169 tasks). Reports point means only; no CIs, no equivalence test; does not port a benchmark between harnesses.
why: Title matches the search phrase 'same benchmark, different harness' but content is a harness-config ablation, not port validation.

title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
summary: Shows that changing a coding agent's harness (context management under pressure) with a fixed model changes SWE-bench Verified/Pro outcomes substantially (28% to 49% per-task fail-to-pass on a 169-task cohort); argues model and harness must be evaluated together. Full text has no Harbor/parity/equivalence mentions.
why: Supports the premise that harness differences move scores, but compares two configurations of one harness rather than an original benchmark and its port.

title: Same Output, Different Gold: Measuring How Reference Choice Moves a Multilingual Benchmark Score
summary: Holds system output fixed and swaps the reference annotation on a six-language PII benchmark; score moves 2-5 F1 (95% CIs reported) and a paired reference-by-system interaction of +2.95 changes one language's margin; proposes reporting a reference-sensitivity band.
why: Neighbour on how an implementation detail of a benchmark moves scores by 'a few points', with CIs; not about ports or agents.

title: Show Your Work: Improved Reporting of Experimental Results (Dodge et al.)
summary: Expected-validation-performance reporting; variance across hyperparameter/seed budgets.
why: Variance-reporting neighbor.

summary: Signal-to-noise framework for choosing benchmarks that reliably separate models.
why: Eval-noise neighbor.

title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness
summary: Position paper (Zhang et al.). 'Binding Constraint Thesis': for long-horizon tasks harness configuration explains more variance than model choice; evidence includes a controlled variance decomposition with model-ranking reversals and figures such as Opus 4.5 at 45.9% vs 55.4% on SWE-bench Pro under different scaffolds; proposes Harness Cards, a locked-harness or factorial protocol, and a disclosure standard. Abstract has nothing on ports, adapters, parity, equivalence tests or CIs.

title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness
summary: Position paper: harness-induced variance can exceed model-induced variance and reverse model rankings (Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 moved 69.7% to 77.0% by harness alone per the search snippet). Harbor appears only as a citation; no parity experiments, range overlap, SEM or equivalence test.

title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness (arXiv 2605.23950, ICML 2026 position paper)

title: Tempered Expectations: A Tutorial for Calculating and Interpreting Prediction Intervals in the Context of Replications
source: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (Spence & Stanley)
summary: States that popular replicability checks such as 'comparing significance levels across studies or eyeballing confidence intervals' are ill-suited, and presents prediction intervals (with an R package) to decide whether a replication is inconsistent with the original. Cites Belia 2005.
why: Cross-field precedent that eyeballed interval overlap is the wrong replication criterion; a prediction-interval alternative the paper could mention alongside TOST.

title: Terminal-Bench Leaderboard Rankings: Luck or Skill?
summary: Confirmed: LessWrong personal-blog post by user 'nateg551015', posted 2026-08-05 21:20 UTC, score 7, 0 comments. Uses public Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard data (tbench.ai, via the yoonholee/terminalbench-trajectories dataset; 89 tasks, >=5 tries per task, 52,104 trials, 325 agent pairs). Task-clustered bootstrap CIs and pairwise tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q=0.05), ICC(1) for run-to-run reliability (0.5-0.8). Findings: 24/25 adjacent-rank pairs are within noise; 23% of all pairs 'statistically equivalent' (meaning non-significant, not a formal equivalence test); scaffold choice moves scores by 4-22 points per model. (a) Harbor parity: NO (Harbor named once, in a licence note). (b) Ports: NO. (c) Equivalence testing: NO; it conflates non-significance with equivalence.
why: Leaderboard-noise neighbor on the same ecosystem (Terminal-Bench/Harbor data), useful as a concrete example of the absence-of-evidence fallacy our paper addresses; it does not look at ports or parity experiments.

title: Terminal-Bench Leaderboard Rankings: Luck or Skill? (LessWrong post by nateg551015)

Notes naive trial-level independence halves the CI width. Zero comments. No mention of adapters, ports or parity.

title: Terminal-Bench Leaderboard Rankings: Luck or Skill? (LessWrong, nateg551015)

summary: Argues agent benchmark scores reflect scaffold decisions and scorer validity; audit-and-repair protocol with seeded ground-truth scoring and worst-case/tail metrics on ComtradeBench. Full text: no parity, Harbor or equivalence-test mentions.

title: Statistics notes: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence
summary: Corrected citation: Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1995). Statistics notes: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ, 311(7003), 485. DOI 10.1136/bmj.311.7003.485 (19 August 1995; PMID 7647644, PMCID PMC2550545). Verified via Crossref (both authors, vol 311 issue 7003 page 485, issued 1995-08-19) and the PMC record (title, authors, Medical Statistics Laboratory, ICRF London). One-page note: a non-significant trial shows absence of evidence of a difference, not evidence of no difference, usually because of inadequate power. The bmj.com page was not accessible; PMC has the PDF. No connection to AI evals.
why: Classic reference for the fallacy underlying the range-overlap rule; not competing work.

title: think-step-by-step/deepsynth-harbor-parity and sealqa-harbor-parity (parity forks for adapters)
